newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia hopes for peaceful polls, markets wary.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia hopes for peaceful polls, markets wary.

text.p: Indonesian leaders called on Friday for a peaceful general election campaign as concern over possible violence before the May 29 national and local polls rattled the nation's financial markets.

Official reassurances came at an early morning pre-campaign ceremony involving officials and leaders of the three sanctioned parties as the rupiah slid further against the dollar before stabilising in late morning trade.

"We hope the election campaign will go smoothly," said Interior Minister Yogie Memet, speaking in his role as head of the General Election Institute (LPU), which oversees the campaign opening on Sunday and the polls.
After weeks of violence between rival political factions in populous Central Java province, financial market dealers said foreign exchange markets remained nervous.
Spot rupiah fell to a low of 2,440 rupiah against the dollar on Friday morning after an opening of 2,432.50, but later recovered to around 2,437 by the close in Jakarta.
"The rupiah has settled down for now. But I think the focus is now on Sunday," one U.S. bank dealer said.
"People keep buying the dollar as they try to factor in possible riots or unrest during the campaign," a local bank dealer said.
Armed forces commander General Feisal Tanjung said the authorities had anticipated any problems.

"We are ready. There will be no riots. All is safe," Tanjung told reporters after the LPU ceremony, which included the traditional Javanese cutting of a large cone of cooked rice to bring good fortune for the election.
The military and police have conducted high-profile training exercises to prepare for any contingency, including riots, hostage-taking and bomb threats.
Streets around Jakarta's central Welcome Monument were blocked for 30 minutes on Friday afternoon as rifle-wielding soldiers rappelled from seven helicopters in a mock anti-riot exercise.

Despite recent clashes in Central Java between supporters of the ruling Golkar party and the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), Tanjung said there were no provinces where trouble was expected.
The political temperature increased in Central Java early this year after its governor ordered public buildings and objects to be painted yellow, the colour of Golkar.
The move led to retaliation by supporters of the PPP and Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), which repainted public objects white or red and white.
Clashes in various towns have escalated in recent weeks as each attack sparked retaliation from the other side.
PPP Chairman Ismail Hasan Metareum told a news conference he had called a meeting of local party leaders from across Java in an attempt to organise an orderly campaign.
Golkar is seeking just over 70 percent of the vote from the 124.7-million-strong electorate after gaining 68 percent in 1992 elections. The PPP got 17 percent and PDI 15 percent in 1992.
Metareum said he expected the PPP to achieve about the same vote in this election as it did in 1992, campaigning on the theme of "justice".
"The conditions are about the same as in 1992," he said.
